opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back. The short answer is that the gap between how capable these models are and how robust they are keeps widening, and right now there's no good public scoreboard for the second part.

Look at where we are. Frontier models are being deployed as agents: browsing the web, writing and executing code, handling people's email and files. They have real permissions in real systems. But the security picture has barely moved. In our red-teaming work at FAR.AI we can still reliably get around safeguards on essentially every frontier model we test. Jailbreaks still work, prompt injection is still largely unsolved, and the defenses that do exist tend to be brittle. They hold up against the attacks the developer anticipated and fail against something slightly novel.

Meanwhile, the incentives push almost entirely toward capabilities. Every lab can point to a leaderboard and say "we're number one on this coding benchmark" or "we beat the other models on this reasoning eval." That competitive pressure is powerful. It drives a huge amount of investment. Security has nothing comparable. Labs make claims like "our model is our most robust yet," but those claims are usually based on internal evaluations that aren't comparable across companies, often aren't reproducible, and sometimes use attacks that are already stale.

So part of the motivation is just measurement. If you can't measure something consistently, you can't tell whether it's improving, and you can't hold anyone accountable for it. We wanted a common yardstick: the same adversarial methods, applied the same way across models, kept up to date as attacks evolve, so you get an apples-to-apples comparison.

The other part is shifting incentives. If there's a visible, credible ranking of how hard models are to misuse or hijack, then security becomes something labs can compete on, and something customers and policymakers can actually look at when they choose which model to deploy or how to regulate. Enterprises deploying agents increasingly ask "how easily can this thing be turned against me?", and right now they don't have a good answer.

On timing: this matters more every month because the stakes are rising. A jailbroken chatbot giving bad advice is one thing. A compromised agent with access to your codebase, your finances, or eventually to dangerous scientific knowledge is something else. We want measurement infrastructure in place before the most serious capabilities arrive, not after. It's much easier to build a norm of "you should report your robustness on a standardized, independent benchmark" now than to retrofit it later in a crisis.

r001.rationale: It describes real deployed agents with system permissions and says red-teamers can reliably bypass safeguards on essentially every frontier model tested.

r002.rationale: It says safeguards are brittle and that lab evaluations are incomparable or stale, but does not clearly state that frontier models’ safeguards have not undergone systematic evaluation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that the gap between what labs say about their models' security and what anyone outside can actually verify has gotten uncomfortably wide. Every frontier release ships with a system card claiming the model is robust to jailbreaks, resistant to misuse, hard to extract dangerous information from. But those claims are made by the people selling the product, using evaluations they designed, on test sets they chose. There's nothing wrong with labs doing that work, but it shouldn't be the only data point.

What we've found at FAR, running red-teaming across many of these systems, is that the headline numbers often don't survive contact with a motivated adversary. A model that scores well on a standard jailbreak benchmark can fall over when you adapt the attack slightly, or when you chain techniques, or when you simply spend more compute searching. And those results tend to stay in private reports or get disclosed quietly to one lab at a time. So the public, policymakers, enterprise buyers, they're all operating on vendor marketing.

A leaderboard changes the incentive structure. If robustness is measured consistently, by a third party, with attacks that are adaptive rather than static, then security becomes something you can compete on. Right now you can't. There's no commercial reason to be more robust than your competitor if nobody can tell the difference. We saw this dynamic in other fields: browser security, car safety ratings. Once there was an independent score, the whole industry moved.

The timing matters because these models are being wired into agents with real permissions, real tools, access to money and infrastructure. The cost of a jailbreak is no longer an embarrassing screenshot. It's a compromised system. And the window where we can establish norms around independent measurement, before deployment gets too entrenched to change, feels like it's closing. So we'd rather build the thing now, imperfect as a first version will be, than wait until the stakes are even higher.

r001.rationale: The response describes jailbreak weaknesses found through red-teaming and warns of possible compromised systems, but does not identify AI-enabled malicious activity as an observed real-world problem.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes labs’ evaluations as self-designed and argues for consistent third-party measurement, but it does not state that frontier models’ safeguards have not undergone systematic evaluation.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real gap between how we measure what AI systems can do and how we measure whether they’re secure. We have lots of benchmarks for capabilities, but if you’re deploying a model, you also need to know: what happens when someone is actively trying to make it fail?

That’s a different question from whether it behaves well in ordinary use. A system can look very reliable with cooperative users and still have vulnerabilities that an attacker can exploit repeatedly. And as we give models access to tools, sensitive information, and more consequential workflows, that distinction becomes much more important.

The goal of an AI security leaderboard is to make those risks easier to assess and compare. We want to give developers a useful signal about where their defenses need work, and give users a better basis for choosing systems. A leaderboard can’t establish that a model is secure, but it can help move the conversation from broad claims about safety toward concrete evidence of how systems hold up under attack.

r001.rationale: The response describes attackers exploiting vulnerabilities as a deployment concern, but does not say AI-enabled malicious activity has been observed in the real world.

r002.rationale: It calls for better security assessment but does not state that frontier models’ safeguards have not been systematically evaluated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real gap between how capable AI systems are becoming and how well we understand their security. We have lots of benchmarks for whether a model can solve a coding problem or answer a difficult question, but much less clarity on whether it will still behave as intended when someone is actively trying to make it fail.

That matters more as we give these systems access to tools, sensitive information, and the ability to take actions. A model can perform very well under normal conditions and still be vulnerable to an attacker.

The motivation for the leaderboard is to make that security question more concrete: give developers and users a way to compare defenses under adversarial testing, and give researchers a clearer target for improving them. It’s not a certificate that a system is secure. It’s a way to measure progress and expose where we still have work to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses vulnerability under active attacks as a concern, but does not identify AI-enabled malicious activity as an observed real-world problem.

r002.rationale: The response says security is less clear and calls for adversarial testing, but does not state that frontier models’ safeguards have not undergone systematic evaluation.
